 Mike Flanagan: “The world changes so much, but the fundamentals stay the same”
 Louisville Public Media | 
 By
 Kyle Meredith 
 Published October 29, 2026 at 10:09 PM EDT
 Facebook 
 Bluesky 
 Twitter 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 Youtube 
 Mike Flanagan on Reimagining Carrie, Teenage Cruelty, and Stephen King’s Biggest Question
 Mike Flanagan has a strange relationship with beloved horror classics. He loves them, respects them, and occasionally decides to put himself through the considerable misery of making another version. And the first person who needs convincing is Mike Flanagan.
 “Everybody goes, ‘No, what are you doing?’” he laughed during our conversation about his new Prime Video adaptation of Stephen King’s Carrie. “And then I spend a year going, ‘No, wait. It’s going to be okay. It’s going to be okay.’ I think I’ve got a penchant for nausea.”
 Between Carrie and his upcoming take on The Exorcist, Flanagan admitted it had been a particularly strange year. But the filmmaker behind The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass, and Doctor Sleep wasn't interested in simply giving another familiar story a fresh coat of blood.
 “We were never interested in supplanting or replacing or trying to improve upon the book or De Palma’s masterpiece,” he explained. “It was really like, no, there’s something new and different we can do with this that could be really cool and really timely.”
 That distinction matters when you're dealing with a story that's been terrifying audiences for half a century. King's original novel arrived in 1974, Brian De Palma's film followed in 1976, and the image of a blood-soaked teenage girl at prom has become practically impossible to separate from American horror.
 Flanagan understood the skepticism because he shared it. “I have an immediate kind of reaction to those ideas when they come up where it’s like, why? Why leave it alone? If I don’t have a fantastic answer for why, I pass on the project. And with something like this, where I’ve got to bring it to Stephen King, whose first question is also why, if I don’t have a terrific answer, then I’m not going to do it.”
 He wasn't approaching the material as someone who thought he knew better than the people who loved it.
 “I’m a fan. I’m a cinephile. I’m just as protective of the books and the movies that I love as anyone else. So I tend to have the same first reactions everybody does. It’s only when I’ve got an answer that I’m really compelled by that I kind of wince and grit my teeth and go, ‘I’m going to do this. I’m sorry.’ And hope that it goes well.”
 The answer, in this case, involved something more frightening than telekinesis: being a teenager in 2026.
 Flanagan's eight-episode adaptation follows Carrie White, played by Summer H. Howell, as she enters public high school after a sheltered childhood under the control of her mother, Margaret, played by Samantha Sloyan. The familiar cruelty remains, but bullying now comes with an audience that can fit inside a smartphone. Humiliation isn't confined to the school hallway anymore.
 For Flanagan, figuring out what that experience actually feels like required more than remembering his own adolescence. He brought teenagers directly into the writers' room.
 “We brought teens into the writer room to talk to us about their experiences and what they would want to see on the screen,” he said. “I learned so much about even my own kids. My oldest son was about to start high school when I started developing this, and it’s led to conversations and revelations about his world and what he goes through that I never, I think, would have had otherwise.”
 The experience also gave him an unexpected appreciation for the emotional endurance required of today's high school students.
 “An enormous amount of respect for the fortitude his generation needs to have every day,” he said. “This has been quite an education for me.”
 There was another connection hiding in the project, too. Asked whether Carrie offered an opportunity to revisit some of the teenage storytelling he'd hoped to continue with The Midnight Club, Flanagan acknowledged that the two projects shared some creative DNA.
 “I hadn't thought about that. I think in some ways, sure,” he admitted. “The Midnight Club, I was so excited about that one. I wish it would have kept going. But that was the first time I was trying to tell stories specifically kind of from the teenage perspective.”
 And while Carrie offered a different kind of story, the opportunity to understand young people rather than simply write about them became central to its development.
 The conversation eventually turned to John Hughes and The Breakfast Club, which Flanagan immediately identified as one of his favorite films. It's an interesting comparison. Hughes understood that the social divisions of high school could be genuinely devastating without anybody needing to levitate the furniture. King simply gave that devastation a body count.
 Flanagan recognized the connection, particularly the way teenage experiences change while the underlying emotions remain stubbornly familiar.
 “The specifics of the teenage experience change so fast,” he explained. “I was in high school in the '90s. Utterly unrecognizable from what it is today, which is utterly unrecognizable from what it was in the '70s, when Stephen King was writing about it.”
 The setting changes. The technology changes. The methods of torment become more efficient. But the machinery underneath keeps running.
 “The world changes so much, but the fundamentals stay the same. Kindness, cruelty, torment, bullying, the importance of empathy, and the potential for violence. All of that is there. It just amplifies and I think just feels more dire today than ever.”
 Which might be the strongest argument yet for revisiting Carrie. Fifty years later, the kids have new ways to be terrible to one another. The terrifying part is how little else has changed.
